stemBlocks.value: Complete the square for x² − 6x + 13 and hence state the minimum value of the expression.
Think first: A square can never be negative, so the smallest the expression can be is whatever is left when the square is zero.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p102-q09 from workbook page 102.

solutionSteps.instruction: Halve the coefficient of x and square it.
Substitute this back into the expression.
Note that a square is never negative, so the expression is smallest when the square is zero.

strategyBlocks.value: Write the expression as (x − 3)² + k, then argue that the minimum occurs when the bracket is zero.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: x² − 6x + 13 = (x − 3)² + 4; the minimum value is 4, occurring at x = 3.

whyThisWorks.value: Once a quadratic is written as a square plus a constant, the square carries all the variation and the constant sets the floor. Since (x − 3)² is zero at x = 3 and positive everywhere else, the expression is never smaller than 4. That constant is exactly the y-coordinate of the vertex of the parabola.

commonErrors.misconception: Stating the minimum as x = 3 instead of 4 — x = 3 is where the minimum occurs, not the minimum itself.
